# Course Description

Econometrics uses statistical methods and economic data to answer empirical
questions in economics. We are interested in three kinds of questions.
(1) How do we test an economic hypothesis? (Example: are men paid more than
women with equivalent levels of education?)
(2) How do we measure a causal effect? (Example: how much does one more year of
schooling raise wages?)
(3) What are good methods of forecasting? (Example: what will the inflation rate 
be next year?)

Questions (1) and (2) are the focus of ECON 399 (and ECON 497). Distinguishing
causation from correlation is the central challenge of econometrics. Question (3)
is the subject of ECON 409/493 — we cover prediction with regression models, but
not time-series forecasting or machine learning.

# Learning Goals

The main tool we learn is multiple regression analysis. By the end of the
course, students should be able to:
(1) specify, estimate, and interpret regression models, and test hypotheses
about their parameters;
(2) judge when a regression estimate supports a causal claim, and diagnose the
common problems — omitted variable bias and other sources of endogeneity,
heteroskedasticity, etc. — that arise in practice; and 
(3) use R to carry out an empirical analysis from raw data to final results.

# Course Prerequisites and Corequisites

Prerequisites: ECON 281, 282 and 299 or equivalent, and MATH 156 or equivalent.
These pre/corequisites are enforced by the department. If you do not have these
pre/corequisites your registration may be cancelled.

The course uses basic probability and statistics and elementary calculus
throughout; Appendices A–C of Wooldridge cover the expected background.

# Textbooks

Wooldridge (2019, 7th edition) will be our main reference. The course follows
this textbook closely, and all chapter references in this outline are to the 7th
edition (older editions can also be used).

- Wooldridge, J.M. (2019). *Introductory Econometrics: A Modern Approach*,
  7th edition. Cengage.

In addition, two R companions are available free online (neither is a substitute
for Wooldridge):

- Heiss, F. (2020). *Using R for Introductory Econometrics*, 2nd edition. \
  Available here: <http://www.urfie.net> (follows Wooldridge chapter by chapter).

- Hanck, C., Arnold, M., Gerber, A., and Schmelzer, M. (2021).
  *Introduction to Econometrics with R*. \
  Available here: <https://www.econometrics-with-r.org>.

# Econometrics Package

R is used extensively in the course. R is a free software environment for
statistical computing and graphics (<http://www.r-project.org>), typically used
through RStudio (also free). No prior experience with R is assumed. We will use
the packages `wooldridge` (all textbook data sets), `AER`, and `ggplot2`; each
handout also ships with its data as CSV files.

# Lab Sessions

As part of the course you will learn how to use R. Weekly lab sessions provide 
short guided exercises introducing the R skills needed for the homework 
assignments. Lab attendance is highly encouraged but not graded. The lab 
schedule will be posted on Canvas.

# Missed / Deferred Exams

Deferral of term work is a privilege and not a right; there is no guarantee that
a deferral will be granted. Misrepresentation of facts to gain a deferral is a
serious breach of the *Code of Student Behaviour*.

There will be no make-up midterm exams. A student who misses a midterm exam
because of incapacitating illness, severe domestic affliction or other
compelling reason (including religious conviction) may have its percentage
weight transferred to the final exam. In that case, the student's final exam
will be different from that for the rest of the class: it will contain
additional questions covering the material of the missed midterm.

A student who misses the final exam because of incapacitating illness, severe
domestic affliction or other compelling reason (including religious conviction)
may apply for a deferred final exam. Students seeking a deferred exam need to
apply to their own Faculty; the instructor does not have the authority to
approve such applications.

# Laptops and Phones

In class, notes go on paper and screens stay away: \textbf{laptops and phones 
are not permitted during lectures}. Tablets are okay when they lie flat on 
the desk and are used as a notebook. Students who need a device as part of 
an *approved* accommodation plan should contact me.

This policy is based on evidence rather than preference. The best study we have
on the question is a randomized experiment run in an economics course at West
Point, where sections that allowed laptops went on to score lower on the final
exam than sections that banned them ([Carter et al.,
2017](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.econedurev.2016.12.005)). Other research finds
that the distraction is not limited to the person using the device: students
who can merely see a neighbour's screen also do worse on tests ([Sana et al.,
2013](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2012.10.003)), and when schools in
England banned phones, test scores rose, with the largest gains among the
weakest students ([Beland and Murphy,
2016](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.labeco.2016.04.004)). We will discuss this
evidence, and what makes it credible, in the course.

# Course Outline

The course runs in three blocks. Each block ends with a homework assignment
followed by an exam. Chapter references are to Wooldridge (7th edition).

## Block 1 · Simple Regression

```{=latex}
\begin{enumerate}[label={\color{slate}\firamedium\arabic*.}, leftmargin=2em, itemsep=5pt]
\item \textbf{What is econometrics?} The steps of an empirical analysis; the
      structure of economic data; causality and the notion of ceteris
      paribus.\chref{Ch.~1}
\item \textbf{The simple regression model: estimation.} Derivation and
      properties of the ordinary least squares estimates; goodness of fit;
      units of measurement and functional form; regression and
      causality.\chref{Ch.~2}
\item \textbf{The simple regression model: properties of OLS.} Unbiasedness;
      sampling variance of the OLS estimators; consistency and large-sample
      behaviour.\chref{Ch.~2, 5}
\item \textbf{The simple regression model: inference.} Sampling distributions
      of the OLS estimators; testing hypotheses; confidence intervals;
      reporting regression results.\chref{lecture notes}
\end{enumerate}
```

## Block 2 · Multiple Regression

```{=latex}
\begin{enumerate}[label={\color{slate}\firamedium\arabic*.}, leftmargin=2em, itemsep=5pt, start=5]
\item \textbf{Multiple regression analysis: estimation.} Mechanics and
      interpretation of ordinary least squares; omitted variable bias;
      efficiency of OLS: the Gauss--Markov theorem.\chref{Ch.~3}
\item \textbf{Multiple regression analysis: inference.} $t$ tests; confidence
      intervals; testing multiple restrictions: the $F$ test.\chref{Ch.~4}
\item \textbf{Multiple regression analysis: further issues.} Data scaling;
      functional form; goodness of fit and selection of regressors;
      prediction.\chref{Ch.~6}
\item \textbf{Qualitative information.} Single and multiple binary (dummy)
      variables; interactions; a binary dependent variable: the linear
      probability model.\chref{Ch.~7}
\end{enumerate}
```

## Block 3 · Complications

```{=latex}
\begin{enumerate}[label={\color{slate}\firamedium\arabic*.}, leftmargin=2em, itemsep=5pt, start=9]
\item \textbf{Heteroskedasticity.} Consequences of heteroskedasticity for OLS;
      heteroskedasticity-robust inference; testing for heteroskedasticity;
      weighted least squares estimation.\chref{Ch.~8}
\item \textbf{Serial correlation.} Properties of OLS with serially correlated
      errors; testing for serial correlation; correcting for serial
      correlation; robust inference after OLS.\chref{Ch.~12}
\item \textbf{Endogeneity and causality.} Internal validity; selection bias;
      instrumental variables; difference-in-differences.\chref{Ch.~15, 13}
\item \textbf{More on specification and data problems.} Functional form
      misspecification; outlying observations.\chref{Ch.~9}
\end{enumerate}
```

# Student Responsibilities

\begingroup\small

**Generative AI:**
Generative AI tools (ChatGPT, Claude, Copilot, and similar) are permitted in
this course the way a textbook, a classmate, or office hours are: use them to
ask questions, review material, and get unstuck — including on R code in the
labs and homework assignments. The work you submit must be your own: write up
your homework answers yourself, and do not submit AI-generated text,
derivations, or code that you cannot explain. AI use is not permitted during
exams.

Before outsourcing your homework to AI, consider the design of the course: the
homework (10% of the grade) is rehearsal for the exams (90%), which are written
in person without AI. Recent large-scale evidence finds that pupils who did
their homework with generative AI scored better on the homework but worse on
the exams ([Strömberg et al.,
2026](https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=6868618)). 

Misrepresenting AI-generated work as your own is an academic offence under the
University of Alberta *Code of Student Behaviour* and will be treated like any
other form of cheating or plagiarism.

**Academic Integrity:** The University of Alberta is committed to the highest
standards of academic integrity and honesty. Students are expected to be
familiar with these standards regarding academic honesty and to uphold the
policies of the University in this respect. Students are particularly urged to
familiarize themselves with the provisions of the Code of Student Behaviour
(online at www.governance.ualberta.ca) and avoid any behaviour which could
potentially result in suspicions of cheating, plagiarism, misrepresentation of
facts and/or participation in an offence. Academic dishonesty is a serious
offence and can result in suspension or expulsion from the University.

All students should consult the Academic Integrity website. If you have any
questions, ask your instructor.

An instructor or coordinator who is convinced that a student has handed in work
that he or she could not possibly reproduce without outside assistance is
obliged, out of consideration of fairness to other students, to report the case
to the Associate Dean of the Faculty. See the Academic Discipline Process.

**Recording of Lectures:** Audio or video recording, digital or otherwise, of
lectures, labs, seminars or any other teaching environment by students is
allowed only with the prior written consent of the instructor or as a part of an
approved accommodation plan. Student or instructor content, digital or
otherwise, created and/or used within the context of the course is to be used
solely for personal study, and is not to be used or distributed for any other
purpose without prior written consent from the content author(s).

**Recording of Virtual Meetings:** If any sessions are held or recorded on
Zoom, please note the following disclaimer: "Please note that class times for
this course will be recorded. Recordings of this course will be used to allow
